design_detail: Retrospective review of the 70 deaths in Liverpool that the national programme on Substance Abuse Deaths (np-SAD, a register fed by coroners) reported as drug-related deaths (DRDs): 57 deaths that occurred in 2004 (np-SAD annual report) and 28 DRD inquests completed in January to June 2005 (np-SAD surveillance report), with double counting removed (85 listed, 70 kept; 15 duplicates by editors' arithmetic). For each death the authors read Liverpool coroner's and Drug and Alcohol Action Team (DAAT) records and linked the person (initials, date of birth, sex) to the National Drug Treatment Monitoring System and to drug-related criminal-justice databases (Drug Arrest Referral 2003/04 and Drug Interventions Programme 2004/05 in the Methods; Table 1 and its footnote 3 give contact in 2003/04, 2004/05 or 2005/06, reporting issue 9). Deaths are compared across np-SAD's own three categories, 'drug abuser/dependent' (38; called here the problem-drug-use group), 'non-drug abuser/dependent' (21; here the group without problem drug use) and 'unknown' (11), with chi-square or Fisher's exact tests and a Mann-Whitney U test. One results paragraph and one table; no multivariable analysis. Liverpool was chosen because np-SAD reported it had the highest number of DRDs in 2004. The Discussion adds an argument, from cited sources, that the national, np-SAD and European definitions all leave out deaths from injection-related infections. The authors call the study preliminary.
can_establish: What the local drug-related-death count that np-SAD supplied for performance monitoring contained in one city over about 18 months: how many deaths np-SAD itself placed outside its problem-drug-use category, how old they were, what toxicology found, how many were deaths from drug toxicity, how many were of non-residents, and how many of the people had been in contact with drug treatment or drug-related criminal-justice services as found by record linkage.
cannot_establish: How many drug-related deaths any definition misses (only deaths already in the count were examined, so the undercounting argument about infections rests on cited sources); how the same deaths would be counted under the narrower national or European definitions (never applied to the 70); whether the pattern holds outside Liverpool or after 2005 (one high-count city); or which drug caused any death (toxicology is presence only, the share of deaths tested is not reported, and who decided 'death from drug toxicity', and how, is not stated).

sample.recruitment: Not recruited: every death np-SAD reported as a DRD for Liverpool in two of its publications (Methods). np-SAD's wider definition, used for the local performance figures, counts 'relevant deaths' in which psychoactive substances were implicated, whether or not controlled under the Misuse of Drugs Act 1971 and with or without a post-mortem, or in which there was a history of drug abuse, or in which controlled drugs were present at post-mortem (Background, 2nd paragraph, citing np-SAD's surveillance report). Information on each person came from Liverpool DAAT and coroner records and from the two linked monitoring systems (Methods).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: all 57 deaths np-SAD's annual report gave for Liverpool in 2004 and all 28 DRD inquests its surveillance report gave for January to June 2005, minus double counts. No exclusions are described. The study period is given as 1 January 2004 to 30 June 2005 in the abstract and Table 1 title, but the two source lists use different time bases (deaths occurring in 2004; inquests completed in the first half of 2005).
sample.demographics: Men 45 of 70 (64.3%): 24 (63.2%) in the problem-drug-use group, 13 (61.9%) in the group without problem drug use, 8 (72.7%) unknown, p=0.924. Median age at death 42.36 years (IQR 33.28 to 51.35): 38.23 (32.39 to 44.07), 53.59 (44.13 to 65.81) and 41.15 (29.99 to 52.21). Resident in Liverpool 55 (78.6%): 27 (71.1%), 18 (85.7%), 10 (90.9%), p=0.338. Known history of alcohol abuse 22 (31.4%): 10 (26.3%), 7 (33.3%), 5 (45.5%), p=0.569 (Table 1). Ethnicity, employment, living situation, manner or intent of death and psychiatric history are not reported.
sample.attrition: Not applicable (records). 11 deaths (15.7%) were in np-SAD's 'unknown' category because the information was not available (Methods); they appear in Table 1 but are left out of every comparison.
sample.selection_effects: One city, chosen because np-SAD reported it as the area of the UK with the highest number of DRDs in 2004, so not a representative area. A death enters only if a coroner reported it to np-SAD; how completely Liverpool coroners reported is not described. The two source lists mix year of death with year of inquest, so the 70 are not the deaths of a defined period. 15 of the 70 (21.4%, editors' arithmetic) were not Liverpool residents, so the city's count partly reflects where people died or were investigated rather than where they lived.

exposure.measurement: The grouping variable is a register classification, not measured drug use. np-SAD assigns its categories from coroners' information (Table 1, footnote 1): 'drug abuser/dependent' requires a known history of drug abuse and at least one of four criteria: (1) reported by the coroner as known to use illicit drugs; (2) prescribed substitute medication for drug dependence; (3) a non-prescribed illicit drug present at post-mortem; (4) other information in the coroner's report suggesting a history of drug abuse. 'Non-drug abuser/dependent' means none of the four was met; 'unknown' means the information was not available (Methods). The Methods say the 70 were 'categorised accordingly', while the footnote says np-SAD made the classification, so whether the authors re-applied the criteria is not fully clear (the Abstract and the Results attribute the categories to np-SAD). Toxicology is reported as drugs known to have been detected, which did not necessarily contribute to the death (Table 1, footnote 2); laboratory, specimens, screening panels and the number of deaths tested are not stated. Service contact was found by matching initials, date of birth and sex to the treatment and criminal-justice databases; the accuracy of the matching is not assessed.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not reported. Toxicology is given only as presence or absence of heroin/morphine, methadone, alcohol and cocaine, without concentrations.
exposure.polysubstance: Detected at post-mortem, problem-drug-use group against group without problem drug use: heroin/morphine 22 (57.9%) vs 3 (14.3%), methadone 12 (31.6%) vs 1 (4.8%), cocaine 16 (42.1%) vs 0, alcohol 15 (39.5%) vs 11 (52.4%) (Table 1). Combinations are not tabulated. The text says the toxicity deaths in the group without problem drug use mostly involved antidepressants, antipsychotics and opioid analgesics, without counts (Results; Discussion, 1st paragraph). The authors note that heroin and morphine cannot be told apart at post-mortem (Results).

comparison.controls: A comparison inside the count: the 38 deaths np-SAD placed in its problem-drug-use category against the 21 it placed outside it. There is no second register, no enhanced review of the deaths, and no re-count of the same 70 deaths under the narrower national (Drug Strategy) or European definitions.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to the main question. For the group comparison: causes of death other than drug toxicity, intent (suicide, accident, undetermined), prescribed medicines, mental-health history and whether a post-mortem or toxicology was done are not reported.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Being outside the problem-drug-use category means only that none of np-SAD's four criteria was recorded. In that group alcohol was detected in 11 of 21 (52.4%), 7 (33.3%) had a known history of alcohol abuse, heroin/morphine was detected in 3 and methadone in 1 (Table 1).

outcomes.instruments: From coroner and DAAT records and the two linked databases: sex, residence in Liverpool, detection of heroin/morphine, methadone, alcohol and cocaine, known history of alcohol abuse, drug treatment contact and drug-related criminal-justice contact in 2003/04, 2004/05 or 2005/06, death from drug(s) toxicity, and age at death (Table 1).
outcomes.validity_norms: None reported: toxicology methods are not described and the record linkage was not validated.
outcomes.operationalization: 'Death from drug(s) toxicity' includes toxicity from prescribed drugs (Table 1, footnote 4); who decided it (the coroner's conclusion, the pathologist's cause of death, or the authors reading the records) and on what criteria is not stated, and manner or intent is not recorded. 'Recent' contact means a matched record in the 2003/04, 2004/05 or 2005/06 data year. A DRD is whatever np-SAD counted under its wider definition; the paper does not report the ICD-10 codes or causes of the 25 deaths that were not from drug toxicity.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None: 11 comparisons in Table 1 (10 chi-square or Fisher's exact tests and one Mann-Whitney U test), each at p<0.05.

analysis.effect_sizes: Counts, percentages and p-values only; no intervals or effect sizes. Editors' calculations (Wilson 95% intervals): deaths outside the problem-drug-use category 21 of 70, 30.0% (20.5 to 41.5), or 21 of the 59 with known status, 35.6% (24.6 to 48.3); deaths from drug toxicity 45 of 70, 64.3% (52.6 to 74.5); deaths not from drug toxicity 25 of 70, 35.7% (25.5 to 47.4). Toxicity deaths 90.5% in the group without problem drug use against 50.0% in the problem-drug-use group, a difference of 40.5 percentage points (Newcombe 95% interval 15.9 to 57.1; editors' calculation). Median age difference 15.4 years (z=3.942, P<0.001). Every printed p-value reproduces with Fisher's exact test or the uncorrected chi-square test on the Table 1 counts (editors' recalculation), and every percentage and total in Table 1 is consistent with its counts.
analysis.selective_reporting: Not reported, though available in the records the authors read: the causes of the 25 deaths that were not from drug toxicity (19 in the problem-drug-use group), the drugs responsible for the 45 toxicity deaths, intent, how many deaths had a post-mortem or toxicology, and how many of the 70 would have been counted under the national or European definitions.
analysis.power: Not addressed. The group without problem drug use has 21 deaths and the unknown group 11, so percentages carry intervals of about plus or minus 10 to 20 points.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Of the 70 deaths np-SAD reported as DRDs for Liverpool (deaths in 2004 and inquests completed in the first half of 2005), np-SAD placed 38 in its problem-drug-use category, 21 outside it and 11 as unknown. The 21 were older (median 53.6 against 38.2 years), none had linked treatment or criminal-justice contact (against 31.6% and 18.4% of the problem-drug-use group), heroin/morphine, methadone and cocaine were detected less often, and 19 of them (90.5%) died of drug toxicity, against 19 of 38 (50.0%) in the problem-drug-use group. Half of the problem-drug-use deaths in the count were therefore not deaths from drug toxicity; what they died of is not reported. 15 of the 70 were not Liverpool residents.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that the national monitoring system “includes deaths of people who are not drug abusers” (Abstract, Conclusion); this is supported in the register's sense, but the group means only that none of np-SAD's four criteria was recorded by the coroner, not that the person never used drugs (alcohol was found in 52% of them). The abstract presents their different post-mortem drug profiles and absent service contact as findings; both are partly built into the classification, because a non-prescribed illicit drug at post-mortem or substitute prescribing places a death in the problem-drug-use category, so 0% cocaine outside it is expected by construction and 0% treatment contact partly so, which the paper does not say. The abstract adds that the compact definitions fail to include deaths attributable to drug misuse, such as those from blood-borne viruses; this is not a result of the study (it examined only deaths already counted and has no data on infection deaths) but an argument from the definitions and cited figures (16% of deaths among drug-treatment clients in the North West of England due to infections, from the first author's earlier study; hepatitis C in nearly half of people who inject drugs in the UK; an estimated 4% progressing to severe cirrhosis, from a modelling study of people who inject drugs in Scotland, with no time frame) (Discussion, 2nd paragraph). The Discussion calls the investigation preliminary. The conclusion that the true burden of drug-related mortality is unknown is an argument consistent with the data, not a measurement.

timeline.event: Webb et al. analysed cause and manner of death in drug-related deaths recorded by coroners in England and Wales in 2000, including deaths recorded as overdose that had another cause (on the project's drug-deaths list; not read for this card).
This study: composition of np-SAD's Liverpool drug-related-death count, 2004 to mid-2005.

A study of ketamine deaths notified to the same coroner-fed register (NPSAD) describes its inclusion criteria as still covering deaths with only a drug history or a controlled drug present at post-mortem (as recorded on card sc_corkery_2021, written by another reader).

Chen et al. compared Office for National Statistics data with National Programme on Substance Use Mortality data for opioid-related deaths in England and Wales (title as listed; read by another reader in this round).

replication.where_it_stands: No repetition in another area is reported in the paper. The project's reading list for this topic (search-logs/DrugDeaths_DOI-LIST.md, section 1, Known gaps) names this paper and Goldberger et al. (2013) as the only peer-reviewed comparisons of drug-death definitions its PubMed search found, and found no recent paper comparing the European, ONS 'drug poisoning' and 'drug misuse', Scottish and US definitions side by side. The study remains a single-city, single-period illustration that a wide register definition adds deaths outside drug services' reach; its undercounting argument has to be supported from studies that link people who use drugs to all their deaths.

funding.funder: The investigation into drug-related deaths in Liverpool was funded by the Department for Public Health, Liverpool Primary Care Trust (Acknowledgements).
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors declare that they have no competing interests (Competing interests).
funding.affiliations_note: Two authors from the Centre for Public Health, Liverpool John Moores University, whose staff manage the monitoring systems used for the linkage (Acknowledgements); one from Liverpool Primary Care Trust, the funder; one from the Liverpool Drug and Alcohol Action Team, the kind of body whose performance the DRD figures were used to monitor. The conclusion (the figures include deaths outside DAATs' reach) bears on that body's performance assessment. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not a reason to discount; the counts and categories are np-SAD's.

what_would_settle_it: Apply np-SAD's wider definition, the national (Drug Strategy and ONS) definition and the European definition to the same complete set of deaths in several areas and years, from full coroner files, recording for each death the cause and manner, whether a post-mortem and toxicology were done and what they found, and service contact by validated linkage; and, for the undercount, link a cohort of people in drug treatment to all their death registrations to count the deaths from infections and other causes that no drug-related-death definition captures.

domains.domain: 1. Sample frame appropriate to the target population
domains.note: The frame is np-SAD's own list of Liverpool DRDs, which is exactly the target when the question is what the performance figures contained; but it is one city, chosen for having the highest count, and built from two lists with different time bases (year of death, year of inquest).
Every death on both lists was included and double counts removed; no sampling.

The whole local count, but small: 21 of 70 outside the problem-drug-use category is 30.0% with a 95% interval of about 20.5% to 41.5% (editors' calculation), and the group comparisons rest on 21 deaths.

domains.domain: 4. Study subjects and setting described in detail
domains.note: Table 1 gives sex, residence, age, four toxicology findings, alcohol history, service contact and toxicity deaths by category, but not causes or manner of death, the drugs responsible for the toxicity deaths, or how many deaths had a post-mortem or toxicology.

domains.domain: 5. Data analysis with sufficient coverage of the identified sample
domains.note: All 70 appear in Table 1, but the 11 deaths with unknown status (15.7%) are left out of every comparison, and the coverage of toxicology and of the linkage is not reported.

domains.domain: 6. Valid methods for identifying the condition
domains.note: np-SAD's criteria for its categories are stated, but they depend on what each coroner's file happened to record; 'death from drug toxicity' is not defined and who decided it is not stated; the linkage on initials, date of birth and sex was not validated, so contacts may be missed.

domains.domain: 7. Condition measured in a standard, reliable way across participants
domains.note: np-SAD counts deaths with or without a post-mortem, and the paper does not say how many of the 70 had toxicology or which substances were screened, so 'not detected' cannot be separated from 'not tested'; coroners' files vary in content.

Fisher's exact, chi-square and Mann-Whitney tests suit small groups and every printed p-value reproduces (editors' recalculation), but no intervals are given, 11 tests are uncorrected, and the toxicology and contact comparisons are partly built into the classification.

domains.domain: 9. Adequate response rate, or low response rate managed appropriately
domains.note: Records of all reported deaths; no response was required. Missing classification is covered under item 5.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Appraised with the JBI prevalence checklist, as the round brief directs for record-linkage and certificate studies, because the study describes the composition of a death count (no exposure-outcome question that ROBINS-E could address). For what np-SAD's Liverpool figures contained, the study is direct: it reads the count itself and np-SAD's own categories, so the composition (21 of 70 deaths outside the problem-drug-use category; 25 of 70 not deaths from drug toxicity; 15 of 70 of non-residents) can be cited with its small numbers and its single city and period. Confidence is lower for the group comparisons, because the toxicity classification is undefined, toxicology coverage is unknown and the toxicology and service-contact differences are partly circular. It may be cited for: np-SAD's wider definition as described in 2007; the composition of one local count used for performance monitoring; and, attributed to the authors as an argument, that the national, np-SAD and European definitions of the time left out deaths from injection-related infections. It may not be cited as a measurement of undercounting (no deaths outside the count were examined), for other places or later years, or for which medicines caused the toxicity deaths (no counts given).

key_findings.finding: Of 70 deaths np-SAD reported as drug-related for Liverpool, it placed 38 (54.3%) in its 'drug abuser/dependent' category, 21 (30.0%) in 'non-drug abuser/dependent' and 11 (15.7%) as unknown.
key_findings.note: Percentages are editors' arithmetic from Table 1; the text says half were in the first category.

key_findings.finding: The 70 deaths came from two np-SAD publications: 57 deaths that occurred in Liverpool in 2004 (annual report) and 28 DRD inquests completed in Liverpool in January to June 2005 (surveillance report), with double counting removed (85 listed, so 15 duplicates by editors' arithmetic).

Definitions in force: the UK Drug Strategy definition counts a death whose underlying cause is poisoning, drug abuse or drug dependence and in which a drug controlled under the Misuse of Drugs Act 1971 is involved (16,088 such deaths in England and Wales, 1993 to 2004, from ONS); the local performance figures came from np-SAD's wider definition, which also counts psychoactive substances not controlled under the Act, deaths with or without a post-mortem, deaths with a history of drug abuse and deaths with controlled drugs present at post-mortem. The European and England and Wales definitions are described as similar and compact.

np-SAD's rule for its problem-drug-use category: a known history of drug abuse plus at least one of: reported by the coroner as known to use illicit drugs; prescribed substitute medication for dependence; a non-prescribed illicit drug present at post-mortem; other information in the coroner's report suggesting drug abuse. Deaths meeting none are classed as not drug abuser/dependent, and deaths without the information as unknown.

The group without problem drug use was older at death: median 53.59 years (IQR 44.13 to 65.81) against 38.23 (32.39 to 44.07) in the problem-drug-use group, about 15 years, z=3.942, P<0.001 (Mann-Whitney U); all 70: median 42.36 (33.28 to 51.35).
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph; Table 1, row age at death

key_findings.finding: Death from drug(s) toxicity, including toxicity from prescribed drugs: 19 of 38 (50.0%) in the problem-drug-use group, 19 of 21 (90.5%) in the group without problem drug use (p=0.002), 7 of 11 (63.6%) unknown, 45 of 70 (64.3%) overall. So 25 of the 70 counted deaths (35.7%; 19 in the problem-drug-use group) were not deaths from drug toxicity (editors' arithmetic); their causes are not reported. The text says the toxicity deaths outside the problem-drug-use group mostly involved antidepressants, antipsychotics and opioid analgesics, without counts.
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph; Table 1, row death from drug(s) toxicity and footnote 4
key_findings.note: Who decided that a death was from drug toxicity, and on what criteria, is not stated.

key_findings.finding: Drugs detected at post-mortem (not necessarily contributing to death), problem-drug-use group against group without problem drug use: heroin/morphine 22 (57.9%) vs 3 (14.3%), p=0.001; methadone 12 (31.6%) vs 1 (4.8%), p=0.022; cocaine 16 (42.1%) vs 0, p<0.001; alcohol 15 (39.5%) vs 11 (52.4%), p=0.339. All 70: heroin/morphine 27 (38.6%), methadone 13 (18.6%), cocaine 19 (27.1%), alcohol 31 (44.3%).
key_findings.locator: Table 1, toxicology rows and footnote 2; Results, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: The share of deaths with toxicology is not reported, so these are minimum proportions; the illicit-drug differences are partly built into np-SAD's classification (criterion 3).

key_findings.finding: Linked service contact in 2003/04, 2004/05 or 2005/06: drug treatment 12 of 38 (31.6%) and drug-related criminal justice 7 of 38 (18.4%) in the problem-drug-use group; none in the group without problem drug use (p=0.005 and p=0.043) or in the unknown group; 12 of 70 (17.1%) and 7 of 70 (10.0%) overall. Matching used initials, date of birth and sex.
key_findings.locator: Table 1, contact rows and footnote 3; Methods, 1st paragraph; Results, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: 55 of the 70 deaths (78.6%) were of Liverpool residents, so 15 (21.4%, editors' arithmetic) of the deaths in the city's count were of people living elsewhere: 27 (71.1%) residents in the problem-drug-use group, 18 (85.7%) in the group without problem drug use, 10 (90.9%) unknown, p=0.338.

Example of a death in the count: a person over 90 with coronary heart disease who died of myocardial insufficiency with contributory carbamazepine toxicity, classed outside the problem-drug-use category.

The authors argue that the np-SAD, England and Wales and European definitions all exclude deaths from bacterial and viral infections, often transmitted by injecting, and cite (not from this study) 16% of deaths among drug-treatment clients in the North West of England due to infections, hepatitis C in nearly half of people who inject drugs in the UK, and an estimated 4% progressing to severe, potentially fatal cirrhosis (no time frame given); they propose adding deaths from blood-borne infections to the international definition.
key_findings.note: Second-hand figures; the 16% comes from the first author's own earlier study, and the 4% from a modelling study of people who inject drugs in Scotland (reference 11, Hutchinson et al., 2005), which the authors apply to the UK and Europe. This study has no data on infection deaths.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results text says the proportion of DRDs with recent treatment or criminal-justice contact was 31.6% and 18.4%; Table 1 shows these are the proportions in the problem-drug-use group (12 of 38, 7 of 38), while among all 70 DRDs they are 17.1% and 10.0%.
reporting_issues.consequence: A claim about service contact among all counted deaths must use 17.1% and 10.0%; the printed figures are nearly twice the whole-count figures (31.6/17.1 and 18.4/10.0 are both about 1.85, editors' arithmetic).

reporting_issues.issue: The text says heroin/morphine was detected in half of the problem-drug-use group; Table 1 gives 22 of 38 (57.9%). The text also says half of the DRDs were in that group (38 of 70, 54.3%).

The abstract and the Table 1 title give the period as 1 January 2004 to 30 June 2005, but the 70 deaths combine deaths that occurred in 2004 with inquests completed in January to June 2005; deaths in early 2005 without a completed inquest by June are absent, and deaths before 2004 with inquests in early 2005 could be included.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Methods, 1st paragraph; Abstract, Methods; Table 1 title
reporting_issues.consequence: The 70 is not a count of deaths in a defined period and cannot be turned into a rate.

reporting_issues.issue: The paper does not say how many of the 70 deaths had a post-mortem or toxicology, which laboratory or specimens were used, or which substances were screened, although np-SAD counts deaths with or without a post-mortem.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Background, 2nd paragraph; Table 1, footnote 2
reporting_issues.consequence: The detection percentages are minimums over an unknown tested denominator, and 'not detected' cannot be separated from 'not tested'.

reporting_issues.issue: 'Death from drug(s) toxicity' is defined only as including prescribed drugs; who decided it (coroner, pathologist or the authors) is not stated, intent is not recorded, and the causes of the 25 deaths not from drug toxicity are not reported.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Table 1, footnote 4; Results, 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The 90.5% against 50.0% contrast cannot be checked against a stated rule, and what np-SAD's wider definition added beyond toxicity deaths cannot be seen.

reporting_issues.issue: The Background lists among np-SAD's 'relevant deaths' those in which there is a history of drug abuse, without saying which causes of death count as relevant, and Table 1 shows that 25 of the 70 counted deaths were not deaths from drug toxicity; the Discussion says the np-SAD definition excludes deaths from bacterial and viral infections. The paper does not reconcile the two or say whether any of the 25 non-toxicity deaths were infection deaths.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Background, 2nd paragraph; Table 1; Discussion, 2nd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Which non-toxicity deaths the wide definition counted, and whether infection deaths were among them, is unknown; the claim that np-SAD excludes infection deaths should be attributed to the authors.

reporting_issues.issue: The comparisons of illicit-drug detection and service contact between np-SAD's categories are partly circular: a non-prescribed illicit drug at post-mortem and substitute prescribing are among the criteria that place a death in the problem-drug-use category. The paper does not acknowledge this.
reporting_issues.consequence: The 0% cocaine outside the problem-drug-use category is expected by construction (a non-prescribed illicit drug at post-mortem is criterion 3). The 0% treatment and criminal-justice contact are partly so: substitute prescribing is criterion 2, and other treatment or drug-related arrests count only if the coroner's file records them (criteria 1 and 4), whereas the linkage looked beyond that file. None of these is an independent finding; the age and toxicity-death differences are not affected in this way.

reporting_issues.issue: Whether the authors re-applied np-SAD's criteria or used np-SAD's own assignments is ambiguous (Methods: categorised accordingly; Table 1 footnote 1: the classification is made by np-SAD), though only mildly, since the Abstract and the Results also attribute the categories to np-SAD. Minor typographical points: the abstract reads 'cv. 31.6%', and the p-value column heading says 'not a drug user/dependent' where the row label says abuser.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Methods, 1st paragraph; Table 1; Abstract, Results
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the categories should be cited as np-SAD's.

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods name the criminal-justice sources as Drug Arrest Referral (2003/04) and its successor, the Drug Interventions Programme database (2004/05), while the Table 1 row covers contact in 2003/04, 2004/05 or 2005/06 and footnote 3 names the Arrest Referral Scheme in 2003/04 and the Drug Interventions Programme in 2004/05 and 2005/06; the Methods give no years for the treatment database, whose Table 1 row covers the same three years.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Methods, 1st paragraph; Table 1, contact rows and footnote 3
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; cite the years from Table 1 and its footnote (2003/04 to 2005/06).

disagreements.first_pass: The Background describes np-SAD's definition as including deaths with a history of drug abuse, regardless of cause, while the Discussion says the np-SAD definition excludes deaths from bacterial and viral infections; the paper does not reconcile the two or say whether any of the 25 non-toxicity deaths were infection deaths.
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 272 (corrected): the Background does not say 'regardless of cause'; it lists 'relevant deaths' with a history of drug abuse without saying which causes count; Table 1 shows 25 of 70 counted deaths were not from drug toxicity
disagreements.resolution: Confirmed in the PMC text (Background, 2nd paragraph: 'relevant deaths' where psychoactive substances were implicated, where there is a history of drug abuse or where controlled drugs were present at post mortem; no cause is named). Issue reworded; Table 1 added to the page; consequence unchanged.

disagreements.first_pass: the sentence overstates contact in the count as a whole by about half.
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 272 (confirmed, wording): the whole-count figures are a little over half the printed ones, so the printed figures are about 85% too high, not 'about half'
disagreements.resolution: Recomputed from Table 1: 12/38 = 31.6% against 12/70 = 17.1%, 7/38 = 18.4% against 7/70 = 10.0%; both ratios about 1.85. Consequence reworded.

disagreements.first_pass: The 0% cocaine and 0% treatment contact outside the problem-drug-use category are expected by construction and are not independent findings; the age and toxicity-death differences are not affected in this way.
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 272 (confirmed, with a note): strictly true for cocaine (criterion 3); for treatment and criminal-justice contact only partly by construction, so 'expected by construction' is a little strong for those rows
disagreements.resolution: Checked against np-SAD's criteria as printed (Methods, 1st paragraph): a death in the group without problem drug use meets none of the four criteria, so a non-prescribed illicit drug at post-mortem cannot occur in that group; treatment and arrests enter only through substitute prescribing or the coroner's information. Consequence reworded; the matching sentence of interpretation_gap.claimed changed to agree.

disagreements.first_pass: so 0% cocaine and 0% treatment contact outside it are expected by construction, which the paper does not say.
